title: Learned ASD subgroups show exploratory associations with disrupted biological processes
summary: Clustering of clinical measures from 2,446 Autism Genome Project cases identified two ASD subgroups differing in severity, adaptive behavior, intellectual ability and verbal status. Analysis of copy-number variants and brain-gene functions linked the groups to disrupted biological processes. Random-forest importance analysis and a Naive Bayes classifier evaluated these relationships; in a higher-information subset, cluster prediction reached precision 0.82 but recall 0.39. These are exploratory genotype–phenotype associations, without experimental demonstration of causal mechanisms, a validated clinical biomarker or independent cohort confirmation. Missing clinical and functional-annotation information constrained prediction.
ai_technology: Clinical hierarchical clustering; random-forest feature importance; Naive Bayes classification
organization: Instituto Nacional de Saúde Doutor Ricardo Jorge; University of Lisbon; University of Coimbra

evidence.tested: 2,446 ASD cases supplied clinical clustering data; functional enrichment and cross-validated learned analyses evaluated genotype–phenotype associations, with limited recall in the information-rich subgroup.
evidence.unknown: Missing data and incomplete functional annotations constrain the usable subset. Mechanistic causation, diagnostic utility and transfer to independent cohorts are not established.
evidence.ai_role: Clustering learned phenotypic groups; random forests ranked disrupted processes, and five-fold Naive Bayes classification assessed prediction of the groups from those processes.

source_review.scope: Independent primary publisher full-text abstract, clinical/model Methods, feature-importance/classifier cross-validation, relevant Results and Discussion limitations; publisher date/affiliations. No supplement review.
